t: Maximum Genetic Difference Query: Offline DFS with a Binary Trie
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Every node's id is its genetic value; each query [node, val] asks for the maximum of val XOR p over all p on the root-to-node path, node included. In Example 1, query [3,2] considers path values {3,1,0} and 2 XOR 1 = 3 wins; query [2,5] over {2,1,0} yields 5 XOR 2 = 7. With n up to 10^5 and 3*10^4 queries, walking each root-path per query can cost billions of operations. The standard remedy: process queries offline during a single DFS that maintains a binary trie containing exactly the values on the current root-to-node path — insert on entering a node, delete on leaving — so every parked query is answered by one greedy descent of about 18 steps (values <= 2*10^5 < 2^18).
k: Maximizing val XOR p over a dynamic set is a trie classic: descend from the highest bit, always taking the opposite bit of val when it exists.
DFS enter/leave updates with per-node reference counts keep the trie exactly equal to the current path; grouping queries by node makes processing offline trivial.
18 bits suffice since all values fit under 2^18.

a.i: For each query, climb from the queried node to the root using the parents array, XOR each visited value with val, and keep the maximum. This directly encodes the definition, needs no auxiliary structures, and is perfectly fine when both depth and query count are small — but at Q * depth near 3*10^9 operations it will not pass the given limits.
s: Starting at cur = node, repeat while cur != -1:
Update best with val XOR cur.
Store best as this query's answer.
a.t: O(Q * D) where D is tree depth — up to ~3*10^9 operations at the limits, too slow.

a.n: Approach 2: Offline DFS + Binary Trie with Counts (optimal)
a.i: Build children lists from parents and bucket queries by their target node. Run an iterative DFS carrying a binary trie whose entries are the ids on the current root path; each trie node stores child pointers plus a counter so insertion/deletion is symmetric. Entering a node inserts its id, answers that node's queries by greedy bit descent, and pushes an exit marker; popping the marker removes the id. Every query then costs O(BITS) instead of O(depth), and the whole run is linear in nodes times bits.
s: Group query indices by node; allocate a trie of arrays (children[2] and count) sized n * BITS + 2.
Iterative DFS with explicit stack: on first visit insert node value (+1 along its 18-bit path).
Answer every query bucketed at this node via greedy descent preferring the opposite bit when its count > 0.
Push exit marker, then all children; on exit marker decrement counts (-1).
Return answers indexed by original query order.
a.t: O((n + Q) * 18) — each node enters/leaves the trie once and each query does one bounded-bit descent.
a.sp: O(n * 18) — trie arrays dominate; DFS stack adds O(n).

w: Present the brute force to show you understand the problem, then upgrade to offline DFS + trie as the intended solution. Pitfalls: forgetting to answer queries AFTER inserting the node itself (the path includes the node), skipping deletion on exit which inflates counts and corrupts later branches, and deep recursion — Python and Java need explicit stacks for chains of 10^5 nodes. Note the trie must support deletion because subtrees share no prefixes of the path; counters make removal exact even with duplicate values. Follow-ups: online queries force persistent tries or Mo's-style reordering; subtree variants map to Euler tours; XOR-minimum just flips the greedy preference.
